title: The “Unburned Bridge”: A Conceptual Analysis of the Roles of Literature in B. F. Skinner’s Life and Work
abstract: Abstract B. F. Skinner’s engagement with literature has often been portrayed in dismissive terms. In biographical accounts, literary activity is frequently described as a marginal episode associated with an unsuccessful attempt to pursue a writing career, whereas theoretical interpretations have often suggested that literature lies beyond the explanatory scope of Skinnerian psychology. Challenging these interpretations, this article argues that literature constituted an organizing dimension of Skinner’s intellectual trajectory, encompassing both biographical and epistemological aspects. The first section examines the biographical dimension of this engagement, arguing that literary practice functioned as a mediating element in Skinner’s transition from literary aspirations to scientific work, while contributing to the formation of his intellectual identity. Rather than representing a failed career path, literary engagement is examined as a formative experience that shaped his epistemological and conceptual orientations. The second section analyzes the theoretical dimension, identifying three functions of literature within Skinner’s philosophical-scientific project: as a philosophical interlocutor that contributed to his epistemological reflections and critique of mentalism; as an analytical resource for the contextual interpretation of psychological concepts such as self and personality; and as a resource for cultural design, informing his reflections on educational and governmental practices involved in the maintenance and transformation of cultural practices. The analysis suggests that literature constituted an enduring and integrative dimension of Skinner’s intellectual development, connecting biography, philosophy, behavioral science, and social reflection, and contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the scope and ambitions of his philosophical-scientific project.
